result.question: Research and produce a comprehensive, cited technology/architecture report for a standalone macOS desktop app ("Grader") that lets teachers grade anything across all domains/subjects, fully locally for privacy (student PII). Key research areas: (1) Best edge/local LLMs for grading + pedagogy expertise, including vision-capable models — evaluate Gemma 3n E2B/E4B, MiniCPM-V 4.5/4.6, Qwen3-VL, InternVL, Granite-Docling, and any newer strong small models; prefer MLX-compatible models for Apple Silicon (mlx-lm, mlx-vlm) vs Ollama packaging; fine-tuning with LoRA/QLoRA adapters for teacher calibration. (2) Document parsing pipeline: Docling, docling + granite-docling VLM, marker, unstructured, PDF/DOCX/PPTX/XLSX/handwriting OCR read AND write capabilities. (3) Web search + crawling for verifying cited references in student work: crawl4ai, Playwright, Firecrawl (local options preferred), SearXNG or other local/private search options. (4) App platform: Deno Desktop 2.9 (https://docs.deno.com/runtime/desktop/) viability vs Tauri/Electron/Swift for bundling a local LLM (Ollama or MLX runtime) inside a Mac app; packaging/signing/notarization considerations for shipping model weights. (5) Agent framework: Pydantic AI v2 (https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-ai-v2, https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) for the grading agent with local model providers (Ollama/OpenAI-compatible/MLX), structured outputs for rubric scores, tool calling with small local models. (6) Canvas LMS integration: pulling submissions and writing back grades/comments via the Canvas REST API — submission download, SpeedGrader-style workflows, rubric APIs. (7) Grading agent design: teacher-as-source-of-truth calibration (few-shot examples of graded work, rubric ingestion, source materials as ground truth); pedagogy expertise across disciplines; human-in-the-loop review UX; LLM-grading reliability/consistency research. Deliverable: recommended architecture + model choices with tradeoffs, all claims cited.
result.summary: A fully-local macOS Grader app is architecturally feasible today with the following verified stack: MiniCPM-V 4.5 (8B, OpenCompass 77.0, strong OCR/handwriting per vendor benchmarks) as the primary local vision-language grading model served via Ollama or llama.cpp, with the 1.3B MiniCPM-V 4.6 as an efficiency fallback and MiniCPM-o 4.5 or Granite-Docling-258M (inside the Docling pipeline, DocTags -> Markdown/JSON/HTML) for document parsing of student submissions. Pydantic AI is a verified fit for the grading agent: it supports Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible local endpoint (including MLX servers), and its schema-validated structured outputs with automatic retry directly enable reliable rubric-score JSON — though its default Tool Output mode depends on the local model's tool-calling ability. Deno Desktop (new in Deno 2.9.0, experimental) is a real packaging option producing a self-contained ~40 MB binary using the native macOS WKWebView, sitting between Tauri (~2-10 MB) and Electron (~100 MB+); framework size is second-order next to multi-GB model weights. Recent research (arXiv 2606.11477, June 2026) supports the teacher-as-source-of-truth design: VLMs reach 98.4% on handwritten exam-answer recognition (vs 88-91% for YOLO detectors), the open-weight Qwen3-VL-30B reaches 96.7% locally, and supplying the reference solution as a 'weak hint' cuts false negatives to 0.58% — validating answer-key-conditioned grading. Major research areas (Canvas REST API specifics, local web search/crawling for citation verification, LoRA/QLoRA teacher calibration, and broader LLM-grading reliability literature) produced no surviving claims and remain open.

findings.claim: MiniCPM-V 4.5 (8B params, Qwen3-8B + SigLIP2-400M, released 2025-08-26) scores 77.0 average on OpenCompass, which OpenBMB claims surpasses GPT-4o-latest, Gemini-2.0 Pro, and the 9x-larger Qwen2.5-VL 72B — at release the vendor called it the most performant MLLM under 30B parameters, making it the leading candidate flagship local VLM for grading multimodal student work.
findings.evidence: Merged from three claims (votes 3-0, 3-0, 2-1) verified verbatim across the GitHub README, HuggingFace model card, and the formal technical report arXiv:2509.18154: 'surpasses widely used proprietary models like GPT-4o-latest, Gemini-2.0 Pro, and strong open-source models like Qwen2.5-VL 72B ... an average score of 77.0 on OpenCompass ... the most performant MLLM under 30B parameters.' Scores are vendor self-reported on an 8-benchmark aggregate, not independently replicated; the 'under-30B SOTA' status is date-stamped Aug/Sep 2025 and superseded by OpenBMB's own MiniCPM-o 4.5 (77.6-78.2) and Qwen3-VL 8B by mid-2026.

findings.claim: MiniCPM-V 4.5 claims leading OCR performance (OCRBench 89.0, surpassing GPT-4o-latest and Gemini 2.5) and state-of-the-art PDF document parsing on OmniDocBench among general MLLMs — including handwriting, demonstrated via official handwriting demos and OmniDocBench's handwritten-notes category — directly relevant to grading scanned and handwritten student submissions.
findings.evidence: Quote verified verbatim on the HF model card: 'leading performance on OCRBench, surpassing proprietary models such as GPT-4o-latest and Gemini 2.5 ... state-of-the-art performance for PDF document parsing capability on OmniDocBench among general MLLMs.' Technical report gives OCRBench 89.0 and OmniDocBench EN edit distance 0.175. Handwriting support is via demos and OmniDocBench's handwritten-notes document category, not a dedicated handwriting benchmark. Self-reported and dated Aug/Sep 2025 — should not be presented as current SOTA.

findings.claim: MiniCPM-o 4.5 (released 2026-02-03) claims state-of-the-art end-to-end English document parsing on OmniDocBench (0.109 EN OverallEdit), outperforming Gemini-3 Flash (0.155) and GPT-5 (0.218) — the strongest single-model local option for the Grader document-parsing pipeline.
findings.evidence: Quote verified verbatim in the README with supporting benchmark table; corroborated by the HF card and technical report. Scoping matters: SOTA applies to the end-to-end-model category on English only — pipeline tool PaddleOCR-VL scores slightly better (0.105 EN), and on Chinese MiniCPM-o 4.5 (0.162) trails HunyuanOCR (0.125). Vendor self-reported (asterisked entries evaluated by OpenBMB).

findings.claim: MiniCPM-V models ship first-class local deployment paths — official llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM, and SGLang support with int4/GGUF/AWQ/GPTQ quantized variants (16 sizes for 4.5) and mobile deployment on iOS/Android/HarmonyOS — but no official MLX package exists; Apple Silicon MLX use would rely on community mlx-vlm conversions (which currently center on 4.6/o-4.5, not 4.5), so Ollama/llama.cpp is the lower-risk packaging path for the Mac app.
findings.evidence: Merged from two 3-0 claims. README and model card verified: 'llama.cpp and ollama support for efficient CPU inference on local devices ... int4, GGUF and AWQ format quantized models in 16 sizes'; llama.cpp support merged upstream (ggml-org PR #15575), vLLM merged v0.10.2. Grep of the entire model card for 'mlx'/'apple'/'metal' returns zero hits; mlx-community hosts only 4.6 and o-4.5 quants. The oft-cited 6-8 tok/s mobile figure is a 2024 datapoint for MiniCPM-Llama3-V 2.5 GGUF, not the current models.

findings.claim: MiniCPM-V 4.6 (open-sourced 2026-05-11) is a 1.3B-parameter edge-focused VLM (SigLIP2-400M + Qwen3.5-0.8B) that OpenBMB claims beats larger models like Gemma4-E2B-it with ~1.5x the throughput of Qwen3.5-0.8B, and it was merged into Ollama's official model library on 2026-06-25 — a verified ultra-light fallback tier for low-RAM Macs.
findings.evidence: README verified verbatim including both dates; Ollama official-library listing independently confirmed (official namespace, 14.1K downloads, architecture matches 1.3B total). Performance/throughput figures are vendor self-reported with no third-party replication found.

findings.claim: For the document-parsing pipeline, IBM's Granite-Docling-258M (Apache 2.0, Sept 2025, with an official MLX build for Apple Silicon) is a 258M-parameter document-conversion VLM that outputs DocTags — a structured markup separating content from structure, convertible directly to Markdown, JSON, or HTML — and IBM recommends running it inside the Docling library, where it replaces the ensemble of single-purpose table/code/equation/OCR models with one compact one-shot VLM.
findings.evidence: Merged from three 3-0 claims, all verified against the IBM announcement and HF model card: 'ultra-compact ... open-source vision-language model for converting documents ... Apache 2.0'; 'DocTags define a structured vocabulary ... easily converted directly into Markdown, JSON or HTML'; 'The recommendation is to use this model only as part of the Docling library.' The conversion path is verifiable in open-source docling-core. Key constraint: the model card says it is 'not intended for general image understanding' — it is a parsing specialist, so Grader still needs a general VLM (MiniCPM-V) for grading judgment. DocTags was co-developed with Hugging Face (SmolDocling paper).

findings.claim: Recent research validates VLM-based grading of handwritten work and the teacher-as-source-of-truth design: on a 61-exam/3141-position benchmark, general-purpose VLMs reach 98.4% accuracy recognizing handwritten exam answers vs 88-91% for trained YOLOv5 detectors (handling out-of-cell, crossed-out, and cursive answers detectors fail on); the open-weight, locally-deployable Qwen3-VL-30B reaches 96.7% in weak-hint mode, beating GPT-5.2 (95.6%); and a lightweight 'weak-hint' prompt supplying the reference solution cuts the best model's false-negative rate (student-disadvantaging errors) to 0.58% (FN 52 -> 14).
findings.evidence: Merged from three 3-0 claims, all verified verbatim against the full PDF including Table 2 (Qwen3-VL-30B 96.69%, GPT-5.2 95.57%, YOLOv5 90.93%) and the abstract's 0.58% FNR figure. Confidence capped at medium because all three claims rest on a single single-author arXiv preprint (June 2026, not peer-reviewed, self-released benchmark) and the task is narrow — recognizing single answer letters in exam tables, not free-form essay grading. The 98.4%/0.58% headline figures are from cloud Gemini Flash models; weak-hint also raises false positives for some models (Grok FP 1->193, GPT-5.2 FP 5->80), consistent with judge-over-crediting literature — so answer-key conditioning needs FP monitoring in Grader's design.

findings.claim: Deno Desktop ('deno desktop') is an official Deno runtime feature available starting in Deno v2.9.0 (released 2026-06-25, feature #33441), confirming the platform named in the research question exists — but it shipped as experimental, which matters for a production shipping decision.
findings.evidence: Merged from two 3-0 claims. Docs state verbatim '`deno desktop` is available starting in Deno v2.9.0'; the v2.9.0 GitHub release changelog includes 'feat: `deno desktop` subcommand (#33441)' plus macOS Info.plist support. Corroborated by the release blog and third-party coverage (InfoWorld, AlternativeTo). Note: a separate claim listing specific Deno Desktop maturity gaps (missing clipboard/secure-storage APIs, MSI installers, etc.) was REFUTED 0-3 — do not cite those specific gaps.

findings.claim: Deno Desktop's packaging model suits a local-LLM Mac app: it produces a self-contained redistributable per-platform bundle containing app code + Deno runtime, defaulting to the native OS webview (WKWebView on macOS, ~40 MB, full Node/npm compat) with an optional bundled Chromium/CEF backend (~150 MB) for identical cross-platform rendering — the same native-webview-vs-bundled-Chromium axis on which Tauri (~2-10 MB) and Electron (~100 MB+) differ; framework overhead is second-order versus multi-GB model weights.
findings.evidence: Merged from three claims (3-0, 3-0, and one 2-1). All figures verified verbatim in the official comparison table ('~40 MB / ~150 MB (CEF)' vs '~100 MB+' Electron vs '~2-10 MB' Tauri) and the docs' 'Small by default, full Node compatibility' section. Precision caveat from the Backends page: the default webview backend does NOT bundle a rendering engine (it uses the OS engine); an engine is literally bundled only with the CEF opt-in. Size figures are self-reported vendor estimates for baseline apps. The 2-1 split was on the 'bundles a web rendering engine' summary sentence, which the docs themselves simplify.

findings.claim: Pydantic AI directly enables reliable rubric-score JSON from a local grading agent: structured outputs are schema-validated via Pydantic models (also scalars, lists, dicts/TypedDicts/StructuredDicts, dataclasses, and unions) with automatic retry re-prompting on validation failure — but the default 'Tool Output' mode presents the schema as a special output tool's parameters, so it depends on the local model supporting tool calling, with Native and Prompted Output modes as fallbacks for models that don't.
findings.evidence: Merged from three 3-0 claims, all verified verbatim against the repo README ('guaranteed to be a SupportOutput, if validation fails the agent is prompted to try again') and official docs ('the output JSON schema ... provided to the model as the parameters schema of a special output tool'; ModelRetry with configurable retry budget, default 1). The tool-calling dependency is the key risk for small local models — Grader should benchmark MiniCPM-class models on Tool Output vs Prompted Output mode.

findings.claim: Pydantic AI supports fully local model providers — Ollama explicitly (dedicated docs page) plus any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via OpenAIChatModel base_url, with MLX-on-Apple-Silicon listed among OpenAI-compatible providers and custom model implementations supported — so the Grader agent can target a local Ollama daemon or an MLX server (e.g., mlx_lm.server) with no cloud dependency.
findings.evidence: README verified: model-agnostic with Ollama listed and 'you can easily implement a custom model'; official docs confirm OpenAI-compatible base_url configuration, a dedicated Ollama page, and 'Rapid-MLX (Apple Silicon)' among OpenAI-compatible providers. Minor caveat: the Ollama docs note structured-output limitations for some models — a model-capability issue, not a provider-support issue.

result.caveats: Time-sensitivity: nearly all model benchmark claims are vendor self-reported (OpenBMB, IBM, Deno) and none were independently replicated; MiniCPM-V 4.5's 'best under 30B' status is dated Aug/Sep 2025 and its comparison targets (GPT-4o-latest, Gemini-2.0 Pro) were no longer frontier models by July 2026 — treat superiority claims as era-relative and re-benchmark on Grader's own tasks. The handwriting-grading evidence (arXiv 2606.11477) is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint on a narrow task (single-letter answer recognition), and its best numbers come from cloud models; it should not be cited as proof VLMs can grade free-form handwritten essays. Deno Desktop is one month old and explicitly experimental; the claim enumerating its specific maturity gaps was refuted 0-3, so its production-readiness is genuinely unverified in both directions — as was a duplicate MiniCPM OCR claim sourced to the arXiv paper (1-2), though the same facts survived 3-0 from the HF card. Coverage gaps: no surviving claims address several areas the research question asked about — Gemma 3n, Qwen3-VL/InternVL as general graders, LoRA/QLoRA teacher calibration, marker/unstructured and document WRITE-back, web search/crawling for citation verification (crawl4ai/Firecrawl/SearXNG), Canvas LMS REST API workflows, macOS signing/notarization of model weights, or the broader LLM-grading reliability/consistency literature — so the recommended architecture is well-supported on models, parsing, agent framework, and app platform, but those six areas rest on no verified evidence in this report.
openQuestions: Canvas LMS integration was not covered by any surviving claim: what are the verified REST API capabilities and limits for downloading submissions, writing back grades/comments, and rubric assessment (SpeedGrader-equivalent) from a desktop app, and what auth model (API token vs OAuth developer key) suits a teacher-installed local app?

Can MiniCPM-V 4.5/4.6-class models reliably drive Pydantic AI's default Tool Output mode for rubric JSON, or must Grader fall back to Prompted Output — and what is the measured MLX (mlx-vlm) vs Ollama/llama.cpp throughput and quality gap on Apple Silicon for these specific models?

Is LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning for per-teacher grading calibration practical on-device (or via a one-time local training run) for an 8B VLM, versus achieving equivalent calibration purely through few-shot examples of teacher-graded work — no verified evidence surfaced for either path.

What is the best fully-local web search + crawling stack (SearXNG, crawl4ai, Playwright, self-hosted Firecrawl) for verifying cited references in student work without leaking student PII, and how do macOS notarization/signing rules treat an app bundle or first-run download containing multi-GB model weights?

refuted.claim: MiniCPM-V 4.5 achieves leading OCR and document-parsing performance for its class — 89.0 on OCRBench (beating GPT-4o-latest) and state-of-the-art PDF parsing on OmniDocBench among general MLLMs — directly relevant to parsing scanned/handwritten student work in a grading pipeline.

Deno Desktop currently lacks several maturity features relevant to shipping a production desktop app, including native clipboard/secure-storage APIs, a runtime permissions system, Windows MSI installers, Linux .deb/.rpm packages, and Windows auto-update.
